  tm_polygons() +

    legend.position = c("left", "bottom"))
tmap_arrange(basemap, gdppc, asp=1, ncol=2)










0.5 Converting to SpatialPolygonDataFrame

hunan_sp <- hunan_sf %>%
  as_Spatial()



0.6 Geographically Weighted Summary Statistics(GSWW) with adaptive bandwidth

0.6.1 Determine adaptive bandwidth
Cross-validation

bw_CV <- bw.gwr(GDPPC ~ 1,
                data = hunan_sp,
                approach = "CV",
                adaptive = TRUE,
                kernel = "bisquare",
                longlat = T)

TipMy observation



For the adaptive bandwidth, the cross-validation (CV) procedure tests different numbers of nearest neighbours and compares their CV scores. The optimal bandwidth is the one that produces the minimum CV score. In our case, the selected adaptive bandwidth is 22. This means that for each location, the model uses its 22 nearest neighbours when calculating the local statistics. Since the bandwidth is adaptive, the actual geographical distance covered can vary from one location to another. In densely populated areas, the 22 neighbours may be relatively close, while in more dispersed areas, the model may need to search over a larger distance.

TipMy observation



For the fixed bandwidth, the bandwidth is defined by geographical distance rather than by a fixed number of neighbours. Since longlat = TRUE, the distance is calculated based on longitude and latitude coordinates and is expressed in kilometres. During the cross-validation process, some very small bandwidth values may produce an infinite (Inf) CV score because there are not enough neighbouring observations receiving sufficient weights for a stable local estimation. The algorithm therefore continues testing other bandwidth values and selects the distance that gives the lowest valid CV score. Compared with the adaptive bandwidth, the fixed bandwidth keeps the same geographical search distance for every location, although the number of observations included may vary across space.

0.7 Computing geographically weighted summary statistics
The code chunk below computes geographically weighted summary statistics by using gwss () of GWmodel package. The analysis is performed using adaptive distance weighted. The distance is derived using AlC method and the kernel method used is bisquare.

gwstat <- gwss(data = hunan_sp,
               vars = "GDPPC",
               bw = bw_AIC,
               kernel = "bisquare",
               quantile = TRUE,
               adaptive = TRUE,
               longlat = T)

Note gwss support five kernel methods, namely gaussian, exponential, bisquare, tricube, and boxcar. Repeat the code chunk above with different kernel methods and compare their results visually.


0.8 Preparing the output data
Code chunk below is used to extract SDF data table from gwss object output from gwss() fro subsequent geovilisation. It will be converted into data.frame by using as.data.frame().

gwstat_df <- as.data.frame(gwstat$SDF)

Next,cbind() is used to append the newly derived data.frame onto hunan_sf sf data.frame.

hunan_gstat <- cbind(hunan_sf, gwstat_df)



0.9 Visualising geographically weighted summary statistics

tm_shape(hunan_gstat) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "GDPPC_LM",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile",
                n = 5,
                values = "brewer.blues"),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(
                title = "local Mean")) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_title("Distribution of geographically wieghted mean") +
  tm_layout(legend.position = c("left", "bottom"))

title: Spatial Weights and Applications
text:
This exercise uses the 88 county-level units in Hunan to define who is considered a neighbour. I use GDP per capita as the example indicator and follow the workflow from importing the data to calculating spatially lagged values.
The main questions I keep in mind are:

How does the definition of a neighbour change the weight matrix?
How does a county’s surrounding GDP per capita compare with its own value?
What changes when the focal county is included in its own spatial window?




The analysis uses the Hunan county boundaries and the 2012 indicator table supplied in data4.zip. The two files join through the county name.



pacman::p_load(sf, spdep, tmap, tidyverse, knitr)







The import paths below point to this exercise’s data folder. The course paths are shown immediately before each local import.
hunan <- st_read(dsn = "chap08/data/geospatial", 
                 layer = "Hunan")

hunan <- st_read(dsn = "data/geospatial", 
                 layer = "Hunan",
                 quiet = TRUE)




hunan2012 <- read_csv("chap08/data/aspatial/Hunan_2012.csv")

hunan2012 <- read_csv("data/aspatial/Hunan_2012.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)





hunan <- left_join(hunan,hunan2012) %>%
  select(1:4, 7, 15)







TipWhat I noticed



The join keeps one row for each county and adds GDPPC to the spatial layer. The geometry is still in WGS 84, which is suitable for this first map. The distance-based examples use longitude and latitude with longlat = TRUE, so the distances are in kilometres. I compare these with projected distances in my additional check.







basemap <- tm_shape(hunan) +
  tm_polygons() +
  tm_text("NAME_3", size=0.5)

gdppc <- qtm(hunan, "GDPPC") +
  tm_layout(
    legend.position = c("left", "bottom"))
tmap_arrange(basemap, gdppc, asp=1, ncol=2)














TipMy observation



The highest GDPPC values are concentrated around a small number of counties, while many western and southern counties sit in lower classes. The map gives the variable a spatial shape, yet it does not tell me whether neighbouring counties are similar enough to support a clustering claim. That is the reason for constructing weights before calculating autocorrelation statistics.

Row-standardisation makes each county’s neighbour contributions sum to one. TipMy observation



The row-standardised lag is comparable across counties because it averages the neighbours. The binary lag sum is larger in places with more neighbours, so it measures a sum of neighbouring per-capita indicators. This sum is not total GDP, which would require population weights. Adding the focal county to the window moves the result closer to a local context measure that includes both the county and its immediate surroundings.






The weight matrix is part of the analysis question. Queen and Rook describe different forms of contact, fixed-distance and k-nearest-neighbour rules describe different forms of proximity, and row-standardised or binary weights produce different meanings for a spatial lag.
For this Hunan example, GDPPC appears geographically uneven in the map and the neighbouring values are structured enough to justify checking spatial autocorrelation in the next exercise. I would report the selected neighbour rule with the statistic because the result is not independent of that modelling choice.






TipBeyond the Code: The Weight Matrix Is an Assumption



I initially treated a neighbour as a simple yes-or-no relationship. The calculations made the assumption more visible: the same GDPPC values can produce different lag surfaces when I change Queen to Rook, use a distance threshold, or standardise each row. A spatial statistic is therefore not only a property of the data. It is also a property of how local context is defined.

This exercise uses the 88 county-level units in Hunan to define who is considered a neighbour. I use GDP per capita as the example indicator and follow the workflow from importing the data to calculating spatially lagged values.

Row-standardisation makes each county’s neighbour contributions sum to one. title: Spatial Weights and Applications
text:
The weight matrix is part of the analysis question. Queen and Rook describe different forms of contact, fixed-distance and k-nearest-neighbour rules describe different forms of proximity, and row-standardised or binary weights produce different meanings for a spatial lag.
For this Hunan example, GDPPC appears geographically uneven in the map and the neighbouring values are structured enough to justify checking spatial autocorrelation in the next exercise. I would report the selected neighbour rule with the statistic because the result is not independent of that modelling choice.






TipBeyond the Code: The Weight Matrix Is an Assumption



I initially treated a neighbour as a simple yes-or-no relationship. The calculations made the assumption more visible: the same GDPPC values can produce different lag surfaces when I change Queen to Rook, use a distance threshold, or standardise each row. A spatial statistic is therefore not only a property of the data. It is also a property of how local context is defined.

G, F, K and L: How I Distinguish Them









Function
What it focuses on

G

Are existing childcare centres close to other centres?
The observed curve rises faster than CSR at short distances


F
arbitrary location-to-event
Are random locations in the planning area close to a centre?
Larger empty spaces: the observed F curve lies below CSR at relevant distances

NoteMy learning point



I find the G- and F-functions more intuitive, but K and L are more useful for checking whether the conclusion holds beyond the nearest neighbour. That is why I would not rely on only one curve when making a statement about interaction.

title: 2nd Order Spatial Point Patterns Analysis Methods
text:
My Interpretation
Across these plots, I read the observed curves relative to the CSR line and simulation envelope rather than from the curve alone. When a curve sits outside the envelope, it suggests that the childcare centre pattern in that planning area is not behaving like CSR at that distance range. The G and F functions help me think about nearest events and empty space, while K and L give a broader distance-based view.

title: 2nd Order Spatial Point Patterns Analysis Methods
text:
What I Learned

First-order and second-order methods answer different questions: intensity versus interaction.
Simulation envelopes make the plots more useful because they give a practical CSR comparison.
The same planning area can look different depending on whether I use G, F, K, or L.
The interpretation should be tied to distance ranges, not just one overall statement.

title: 2nd Order Spatial Point Patterns Analysis Methods
text:
Limitations
CSR is a simple benchmark, and it does not account for population distribution, residential land use, transport access, or planning policy. The result is useful for describing spatial pattern, but not enough by itself to explain the causes of that pattern.

title: 2nd Order Spatial Point Patterns Analysis Methods
text:
Reflection
Compared with first-order KDE, second-order analysis made me think more carefully about distance ranges. A single statement like “the centres are clustered” is too broad unless I say at what distance and under which study window. The envelopes also helped me read the plots more cautiously because I could compare the observed curve with simulated CSR patterns rather than relying only on visual impression.






TipBeyond the Code: global = FALSE and global = TRUE



The global choice changes which family of comparisons the envelope covers. With pointwise envelopes, I can look at particular distances and ask where the observed curve moves outside the simulated range. That is helpful for exploration because the distance scale is visible.
A simultaneous envelope tests the entire pre-specified distance interval. A pointwise envelope covers each fixed distance separately; searching across many distances changes the overall error rate. I use global = FALSE for the course plots and compare it with global = TRUE below, keeping the simulated patterns and distance interval identical.

extract_kml_field <- function(html_text, field_name) {

  rows <- page %>% html_elements("tr")
  
  value <- rows %>%
    keep(~ html_text2(html_element(.x, "th")) == field_name) %>%
    html_element("td") %>%
    html_text2()
  
  if (length(value) == 0) NA_character_ else value
}

The quick map is useful as a first check because it confirms that the joined attribute can be mapped immediately. At the same time, it feels too plain for communication: the legend, classification, borders, and layout still need design work before the map can support a clear interpretation.




2.4.2 Creating a choropleth map by using tmap’s elements

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile", 
                n = 5,
                values = "brewer.blues"),

The next map uses a fuller tmap composition: filled polygons, title, border, compass, scale bar, grid, and data credits.






TipWhat I Noticed



The dependency ratio map is sensitive to classification. I find the quantile map useful for comparison because each class has a similar number of subzones, but it can also make small numeric differences look more dramatic.

Small multiples make it easier to compare young and aged population patterns without changing datasets between plots.

      values = "brewer.blues")) +

youngmap <- tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024)+ 
  tm_polygons(fill = "YOUNG",
              fill.legend = tm_legend(
                position = tm_pos_in(
                  "right", "bottom"),
                  item.height = 0.8),
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile", 
                values = "brewer.blues")) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_title("Distribution of young population")
                
agedmap <- tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024)+ 
  tm_polygons(fill = "AGED",
              fill.legend = tm_legend(
                position = tm_pos_in(
                  "right", "bottom"),
                item.height = 0.8),
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
              style = "quantile",

  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_title("Distribution of aged population")

tmap_arrange(youngmap, agedmap, asp=1, ncol=2)










2.5.3 By defining a group-by variable in tm_facets()
In tmap 4, title.size is a relative text size. I use 1.1 for the regional facet titles so each title fits its panel.
tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_fill(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
          fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
            style = "quantile",
            values = "brewer.blues")) + 
  tm_facets(by = "REGION_N",
            nrow = 2, 
            ncols = 3,
            free.coords=TRUE, 
            drop.units=TRUE) +
  tm_layout(legend.show = TRUE,
            title.position = c("center", "center"), 
            title.size = 20) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5)

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_fill(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
          fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
            style = "quantile",
            values = "brewer.blues")) + 
  tm_facets(by = "REGION_N",
            nrow = 2, 
            ncols = 3,
            free.coords=TRUE, 
            drop.units=TRUE) +
  tm_layout(legend.show = TRUE,
            title.position = c("center", "center"), 
            title.size = 1.1) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5)














TipMy Reading of the Facets



The regional facets are helpful because Singapore-wide maps can make smaller regions hard to compare. With free.coords = TRUE, each region gets more visual space, so I can inspect internal variation within regions rather than only noticing the largest polygons on the full island map.

title: Thematic Mapping and GeoVisualisation with R
text:
Beyond the Basic Choropleth
The maps above describe where dependency ratio is high or low. I also wanted to check how much of the story comes from the spatial arrangement itself, not just the distribution of the numbers.

Same Values, Shuffled Locations

set.seed(626)

mpsz_shuffle <- mpsz_pop2024 %>%
  mutate(DEPENDENCY_SHUFFLED = sample(DEPENDENCY))

observed_dependency_map <- tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile",
                n = 5,
                values = "brewer.blues"),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Dependency")) +
  tm_title("Observed dependency ratio") +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5)

shuffled_dependency_map <- tm_shape(mpsz_shuffle) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY_SHUFFLED",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile",
                n = 5,
                values = "brewer.blues"),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Dependency")) +
  tm_title("Same values, shuffled") +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5)

tmap_arrange(observed_dependency_map, shuffled_dependency_map, ncol = 2)














ImportantMy Finding



The shuffled map uses the same dependency-ratio values, but it breaks the connection between value and location. The observed map looks more geographically coherent, while the shuffled map looks noisier. This is a useful reminder that a choropleth is not only about the variable distribution; the spatial arrangement also carries information.




Visual Area Bias

valid_pop_area <- mpsz_pop2024 %>%
  filter(!is.na(TOTAL), TOTAL > 0) %>%
  mutate(area_km2 = as.numeric(st_area(geometry)) / 1000000) %>%
  arrange(TOTAL)

least_pop_half <- valid_pop_area %>%
  slice_head(prop = 0.5)

area_bias_summary <- tibble(
  measure = c(
    "Share of mapped land area in least-populated half of subzones (%)",
    "Share of population in those subzones (%)"
  ),
  value = c(
    round(sum(least_pop_half$area_km2) / sum(valid_pop_area$area_km2) * 100, 1),
    round(sum(least_pop_half$TOTAL) / sum(valid_pop_area$TOTAL) * 100, 1)
  )
)

1 Share of mapped land area in least-populated half of subzones (%)  53.4
2 Share of population in those subzones (%)                          12.5








NoteWhat This Changes for My Map Reading



In my output, the least-populated half of subzones takes up 53.4% of the mapped land area but contains only 12.5% of the population. That means the eye can easily overweight large, sparsely populated subzones. For population mapping, I should be careful not to read visual area as population importance.




Does Preschool Provision Broadly Follow Young Population?

preschool2019 <- st_read("data/geospatial/PreSchoolsLocation.geojson",
                         quiet = TRUE) %>%
  st_zm(drop = TRUE, what = "ZM") %>%
  st_transform(crs = 3414)

preschool_counts <- lengths(st_intersects(mpsz, preschool2019))

preschool_by_sz <- mpsz %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  mutate(PRESCHOOL_COUNT = preschool_counts) %>%
  select(SUBZONE_N, PRESCHOOL_COUNT)

provision <- mpsz_pop2024 %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  filter(!is.na(TOTAL), YOUNG > 0) %>%
  left_join(preschool_by_sz, by = "SUBZONE_N") %>%
  mutate(
    PRESCHOOL_COUNT = replace_na(PRESCHOOL_COUNT, 0),
    young_per_preschool = YOUNG / pmax(PRESCHOOL_COUNT, 1),
    has_preschool = PRESCHOOL_COUNT > 0
  )

provision_summary <- provision %>%
  summarise(
    correlation = round(cor(YOUNG, PRESCHOOL_COUNT, use = "complete.obs"), 3),
    subzones_without_preschool = sum(!has_preschool),
    max_young_no_preschool = max(YOUNG[!has_preschool], na.rm = TRUE)
  )

provision_summary

  correlation subzones_without_preschool max_young_no_preschool
1       0.871                         22                   1930



ggplot(provision,
       aes(x = YOUNG,
           y = PRESCHOOL_COUNT,
           colour = has_preschool)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE, colour = "grey30", linewidth = 0.6) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("FALSE" = "#c2410c", "TRUE" = "#0f766e"),
                      labels = c("No preschool", "Has preschool"),
                      name = NULL) +
  labs(title = "Preschool count and young population by subzone",
       x = "Residents in the course YOUNG age group",
       y = "Preschools in subzone") +
  theme_minimal()














TipMy Finding



The correlation between young population and preschool count is 0.871, so the broad relationship is positive. However, 22 subzones with young residents have no preschool point in this dataset, and the largest of these still has 1930 young residents. I would treat this as an exploratory signal rather than a final provision assessment, because demand also depends on age bands, school capacity, and nearby centres across subzone boundaries.

title: Thematic Mapping and GeoVisualisation with R
text:
Takeaway
Different classification and layout choices can change how strongly a choropleth map communicates spatial contrast. For this dependency-ratio example, the same joined dataset supports overview mapping, regional comparison, and focused outlier inspection. I compare the quantile and equal-interval results, then choose a legend and annotations that communicate the same numeric pattern clearly.

title: Thematic Mapping and GeoVisualisation with R
text:
Reflection
The extra checks changed how I read the choropleth maps. A map can look persuasive even when the classification, area size, or spatial unit is shaping the visual message. The shuffled map, area-bias table, and preschool-population comparison help me slow down and ask whether the pattern is genuinely spatial, visually exaggerated, or only a first descriptive clue.






TipBeyond the Code: Classification Is an Argument



The part I kept thinking about is that style = "quantile", style = "jenks", and equal intervals can all use the same data but tell slightly different visual stories. Quantile is useful when I want every class to contain a similar number of subzones, but it can exaggerate small numeric differences. Jenks is better at following natural breaks, but the class boundaries are less intuitive to explain without the data beside the map.
So I should not treat the classification argument inside tm_fill() as only a design choice. It is part of the analysis. If I were presenting one final map, I would show why that classification was chosen and check whether the main finding still holds when the style changes.

title: Geospatial Data Science with R
text:
Takeaway
The workflow shows why CRS checks and geometry operations are central to geospatial analysis. With the current preschool data, the areas with the highest raw counts are not always the same as the areas with the highest density, because compact subzones can have high service concentration even with moderate counts.

title: Geospatial Data Science with R
text:
Reflection
The most important lesson for me is that spatial analysis is not only about drawing data on a map. The geometry type, CRS, and spatial unit all affect what question the code is answering. I also realised that a result can be technically correct but still incomplete if I do not explain whether it is a count, density, buffer area, or spatial relationship.






TipBeyond the Code: CRS Is Not Just a Setting



One detail I would be more careful with after this exercise is the difference between assigning a CRS and transforming a CRS. st_set_crs() is only telling R what the coordinates already mean, while st_transform() actually recalculates the coordinates into another reference system. If I used the wrong one, the map might still draw, but the distance, area, and density calculations could become misleading.
This also changes how I read the outputs. When I calculate preschool density or spatial intersections, I am not only checking whether the code runs; I am checking whether the geometry is in a coordinate system that matches the question. For Singapore analysis, projected metres are much easier to defend than raw longitude and latitude when area or distance is involved.

text:
4.6 Clark-Evan Test for Nearest Neighbour Analysis
The Clark-Evans test compares the observed nearest-neighbour distances with what would be expected under complete spatial randomness. An index below 1 suggests clustering, while an index above 1 suggests a more regular pattern.

4.6.1 Perform the Clark-Evans test without CSR

clarkevans.test(childcareSG_ppp,
                correction="none",
                clipregion= sg_owin,
                alternative=c("clustered"))


    Clark-Evans test
    No edge correction
    Z-test

data:  childcareSG_ppp
R = 0.53532, p-value < 2.2e-16
alternative hypothesis: clustered (R < 1)




4.6.2 Perform the Clark-Evans test with CSR

clarkevans.test(childcareSG_ppp,
                correction="none",
                clipregion= sg_owin,
                alternative=c("clustered"),
                method="MonteCarlo",
                nsim=99)


    Clark-Evans test
    No edge correction
    Monte Carlo test based on 99 simulations of CSR with fixed n

data:  childcareSG_ppp
R = 0.53532, p-value = 0.01
alternative hypothesis: clustered (R < 1)








TipMy interpretation



The rendered Singapore-wide Clark-Evans index is 0.535. Since it is below 1, the nearest-neighbour pattern supports clustering rather than a regular spacing. The Monte Carlo p-value is 0.01, so the result is statistical evidence against CSR. This does not explain why childcare centres cluster, but it does show that the observed spacing is unlikely to be purely random under this simple null model.

TipWhy bandwidth matters



The bandwidth changes how strongly the surface is smoothed. A smaller bandwidth keeps local peaks sharper, while a larger fixed bandwidth makes the pattern easier to read at a broad scale but can blur nearby concentrations. The adaptive KDE is useful here because childcare centres are not evenly spread across Singapore; it keeps more local detail where points are dense and smooths more where points are sparse.

text:
How I Think About the Method Choices








Choice
Why it matters in this exercise
What I watch for




Study window
It defines where points are allowed to occur
Singapore-wide and planning-area results should not be treated as the same question


Projected CRS
Distance calculations need metre-based coordinates
EPSG:3414 keeps nearest-neighbour and KDE distances meaningful


Bandwidth
It controls how smooth the KDE surface becomes
A very smooth surface can hide local peaks; a very sharp one can over-emphasise noise


Kernel
It changes how density is spread around each point
I compare kernels as a sensitivity check, not as the main conclusion









NoteMy learning point



For first-order point pattern analysis, the study window and bandwidth feel just as important as the points themselves. The same childcare centres can look more clustered or more evenly spread depending on the scale at which I summarise them.



My Enhanced View

The focus map is useful because Choa Chu Kang and Tampines are easier to compare when they are shown together with the same symbol style. Tampines appears to have a more visibly distributed set of childcare centres, while Choa Chu Kang looks more constrained by its planning-area shape.

title: First-order Spatial Point Patterns Analysis Methods
text:
Beyond the Basic Density Surface
The KDE map is visually strong, but I should not over-read it as a demand or accessibility map. It shows where childcare centres are concentrated, not whether the number of centres is enough for nearby children or whether families can reach them easily.






ImportantWhat I would check next



The next step would be to bring in child population, residential land use, or walking-network distance. That would move the analysis from “where are centres dense?” to “where might service provision be relatively high or low compared with potential demand?”

text:
Clark-Evans vs KDE
Clark-Evans gives a statistical check of nearest-neighbour spacing, while KDE gives a visual intensity surface. I would not treat them as substitutes. The test helps me ask whether the pattern departs from CSR, while KDE helps me inspect where concentrations are stronger.

title: First-order Spatial Point Patterns Analysis Methods
text:
What I Learned

CRS matters because the main calculations use distance.
ppp and owin are the key objects that let spatstat understand the point events and the analysis window.
KDE is useful for visualising intensity, but the hotspot appearance depends on bandwidth.
Changing the study window can change the interpretation, especially when comparing Singapore-wide and planning-area views.

title: First-order Spatial Point Patterns Analysis Methods
text:
Limitations
The point pattern shows where childcare centres are located, but it does not directly explain the causes of clustering. CSR is also a simple null model, so the result should be read as a starting point rather than a full explanation of childcare service provision.






TipBeyond the Code: Bandwidth Changes the Story



For KDE, I realised the bandwidth is not just a technical input. A smaller bandwidth makes local hotspots appear sharper, while a larger bandwidth smooths the same points into broader regional patterns. Both can be useful, but they answer different reading questions.
I would use a sharper surface when I want to inspect very local concentration, such as whether centres bunch around a few neighbourhood nodes. I would use a smoother surface when the question is more about planning-area level intensity. This is why comparing bw.diggle, bw.ppl, and the fixed/adaptive KDE outputs matters: it helps me avoid presenting one attractive heatmap as if it were the only possible truth.

title: Spatio-Temporal Point Patterns Analysis
text:
I use the 2023 MODIS fire detections on Bangka Island to explore where and when events concentrate. The overall point map, monthly STKDE, daily STKDE, and space-time K-function each give me a different view of the same observations.





My questions are:

Are fire locations spatially and spatio-temporally independent?
Where and when do detections concentrate?
How do monthly marks, daily marks, and smoothing bandwidths change the interpretation?





The local files contain a NASA FIRMS 2023 MODIS extract and a geoBoundaries Bangka-Belitung boundary. I extract the largest polygon, Bangka Island, and retain its fire points. This produces 741 detections. The boundary is an ADM1-derived coastline; the course uses a union of sub-district boundaries. Small edge and bandwidth differences can follow from this boundary version.



I load the packages used for the spatial, temporal, and mapping steps.

               tmap, stpp, tidyverse,
               animation)

               layer = "Kepulauan_Bangka_Belitung")

               layer = "Kepulauan_Bangka_Belitung",
               quiet = TRUE)

kbb <- kbb_parts[which.max(st_area(kbb_parts)), ]

               layer = "Kepulauan_Bangka_Belitung") %>%
  st_union() %>%
  st_zm(drop = TRUE, what = "ZM") %>%
  st_transform(crs = 32748)

      temporal_band,

    ),

    temporal_label = paste0(temporal_band, " days")

Counts of fire-event pairs within selected spatial and temporal bands.










TipMy observation



Close-pair counts necessarily increase as either threshold grows because each larger window contains the smaller one. I use these counts as descriptive summaries of proximity. Establishing excess space-time interaction requires a benchmark that preserves the spatial and temporal margins, together with edge correction; raw pair counts alone cannot establish it.






This exercise helped me see why spatio-temporal point pattern analysis needs both a spatial window and a time mark. The overall map suggests clustering, but the monthly and day-of-year views show when the clustering becomes strongest. In my local extract, the clearest signal appears after mid-year, with the strongest density around the late dry-season months.
Reproducibility requires the data, study window, method, and reported output to agree. I record the boundary source and run the STKDE and K-function directly. Separate two-dimensional density panels give an additional visual comparison, with their own scale limitations.






TipBeyond the Code: Time Marks Need a Scale



For spatio-temporal KDE, I should not treat Month_num and DayofYear as interchangeable time marks. Month is easier to communicate and gives a clean seasonal overview, but it hides within-month changes. Day of year is more detailed, but it creates many more time slices and needs stronger smoothing to avoid turning the page into noisy frame-by-frame output.
The lambda value is therefore similar to bandwidth in space: it decides how much neighbouring time is allowed to influence a density estimate. In my interpretation, a monthly view is good for telling the broad fire-season story, while the day-of-year view is better for checking whether that story happens gradually or through shorter bursts of activity.

title: Spatio-Temporal Point Patterns Analysis
text:
This exercise helped me see why spatio-temporal point pattern analysis needs both a spatial window and a time mark. The overall map suggests clustering, but the monthly and day-of-year views show when the clustering becomes strongest. In my local extract, the clearest signal appears after mid-year, with the strongest density around the late dry-season months.
Reproducibility requires the data, study window, method, and reported output to agree. I record the boundary source and run the STKDE and K-function directly. Separate two-dimensional density panels give an additional visual comparison, with their own scale limitations.






TipBeyond the Code: Time Marks Need a Scale



For spatio-temporal KDE, I should not treat Month_num and DayofYear as interchangeable time marks. Month is easier to communicate and gives a clean seasonal overview, but it hides within-month changes. Day of year is more detailed, but it creates many more time slices and needs stronger smoothing to avoid turning the page into noisy frame-by-frame output.
The lambda value is therefore similar to bandwidth in space: it decides how much neighbouring time is allowed to influence a density estimate. In my interpretation, a monthly view is good for telling the broad fire-season story, while the day-of-year view is better for checking whether that story happens gradually or through shorter bursts of activity.

The main questions I keep in mind are:

text:
This exercise checks whether GDP per capita in Hunan is geographically patterned. I use the global statistics first, then look at how the relationship changes across neighbour orders in the correlograms.
The main questions I keep in mind are:

Are neighbouring counties more alike than a random arrangement would suggest?
Do Moran’s I and Geary’s C tell the same story from different perspectives?
At which neighbour orders does the relationship weaken or change direction?

Geary’s C is below 1 at the first two orders, close to 1 around the middle orders, and above 1 at the fifth order. That change is consistent with the Moran correlogram: the strongest local similarity is short range, and the relationship becomes weaker or reverses as the neighbourhood expands.

The teacher workflow uses Queen contiguity and row-standardised weights. I repeated the global tests with Rook contiguity to see how sensitive the conclusion is to the shared-corner rule.

wm_r <- poly2nb(hunan, queen = FALSE)
rswm_r <- nb2listw(wm_r, style = "W", zero.policy = TRUE)

comparison <- tibble(
  statistic = c("Moran's I", "Geary's C"),
  queen = c(
    unname(moran_result$estimate[["Moran I statistic"]]),
    unname(geary_result$estimate[["Geary C statistic"]])
  ),
  rook = c(
    unname(moran.test(hunan$GDPPC, rswm_r, zero.policy = TRUE)$estimate[["Moran I statistic"]]),
    unname(geary.test(hunan$GDPPC, rswm_r)$estimate[["Geary C statistic"]])
  )
)

TipWhat I learned from the comparison



The Rook check changes the exact statistics because it removes corner-touching links, while the overall direction remains positive Moran’s I and sub-one Geary’s C. This makes the modelling choice visible: the claim is strongest when it includes the chosen neighbour definition, the weighting style and the statistic together.
